Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, predicted he would defeat Republican Mike Rogers by seven points in Michigan’s Senate race, as polls point to a competitive election in the critical battleground for the 2026 midterms.
The prediction by El-Sayed, the former Wayne County health director and a favorite among progressives, comes as he faces questions about whether he would make a strong candidate for Democrats in a swing state that narrowly backed President Donald Trump in 2024.

El‑Sayed Addresses Electability Concerns in Michigan Senate Race
El-Sayed is running in the primary to replace Senator Gary Peters, a Democrat who opted to retire ahead of the midterms.
The race is seen as a toss-up, with both Democrats and Republicans hoping to win it in November.
Republicans believe Trump’s victory two years earlier and a messy Democratic primary could bolster their chances.

Glengariff Group is well known for its polling in Michigan politics.
The poll surveyed 600 likely voters from January 2-6, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points.

Roxie Richner, a spokesperson for El-Sayed, told Newsweek that Michiganders “from all walks of life” are “energized” by his message and that he has “the unique ability to both energize the Democratic base and bring independents and those who have felt behind by the party back into the fold.”

She added: “Not a single poll shows Abdul winning against Mike Rogers.
Michigan can’t afford to lose this critical seat because a man who has never won an election hopes rather than proves he can actually win and deliver for people.”
Joetta Appiah, a spokesperson for Stevens’ campaign, told Newsweek she is “the only candidate in this race who consistently beats Mike Rogers in poll after poll.”
“She outperforms the other candidates because she has earned strong support in Detroit and among Black voters, and stands out as the Democrat who can win over independents.
It’s why she’s leading in the primary, and why she’ll beat Mike Rogers and send him packing back to Florida,” she said.

Michigan Primary Polling Between El-Sayed, McMorrow and Stevens

That poll showed Stevens with 25 percent, El-Sayed with 23 percent and McMorrow with 16 percent support.

Democrats cannot afford to lose Michigan if they want to reclaim control of the Senate in November.
Republicans hold a 53-47 majority, so Democrats must flip four seats to win control.
The vice president serves as the tiebreaking vote.

Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization reporting on voting access and election administration across the U.S.
This news analysis was originally distributed in Votebeat’s free weekly newsletter.
Sign up to get future editions, including the latest reporting from Votebeat bureaus and curated news from other publications, delivered to your inbox every Saturday.
Regrets — we’ve all had a few.
One of President Donald Trump’s, apparently, is not directing the National Guard to seize voting machines after the 2020 election in search of evidence of fraud.
That revelation, part of a wide-ranging interview with The New York Times on Jan.
7, commands particular attention in a world where Trump has already sought to push the boundaries of his power, deploying the National Guard to multiple U.S.
cities to crack down on protests and crime.
The November midterms will be the first federal general election with Trump as president since that 2020 contest, and even before his comments to the Times, plenty of people were already worried that Trump would attempt to deploy the National Guard around the 2026 election.
The National Guard isn’t necessarily the problem here; the Guard actually has a history of helping with election administration, such as when troops in civilian clothing helped fill in for absent poll workers during the pandemic in 2020.
But many Democrats and election officials are worried that Trump could, say, send them to polling places to interfere with voting on Election Day.
If troops were to take possession of voting machines or other equipment, it could break the chain of custody and invalidate scads of ballots.
And if troops just show up outside polling places, even if they don’t try to impede the administration of the election, their presence could still intimidate voters.
That’s a worst-case scenario.
However, there are significant legal and practical barriers to Trump doing this.
First, it’s clearly illegal: Federal law prohibits stationing “troops or armed men at any place where a general or special election is held, unless such force be necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.” It’s also illegal for members of the military to prevent, or attempt to prevent, an eligible voter from voting and to interfere “in any manner with an election officer’s discharge of his duties.” That could include taking possession of voting machines.
Even the Insurrection Act — which grants the president wide leeway to use the military for domestic law enforcement in emergencies, and which Trump threatened to invoke just last week in Minneapolis — wouldn’t give troops the right to break these laws, according to the Brennan Center for Justice.
Second, courts have so far significantly reined in Trump’s existing National Guard deployments — raising questions about whether he’d even have control of the Guard in key states.
In December, the Supreme Court signed off on a temporary restraining order preventing the Trump administration from deploying troops to Illinois, whose Democratic governor had challenged his authority to do so.
(National Guard troops are usually under the command of their state’s governor.)
The Supreme Court’s order for now functionally limits Trump to deploying the National Guard in states where he has the governor’s consent.
And the 2026 midterm elections are likely to be decided in states whose governors mostly aren’t the type to let Trump deploy troops there.
Of the 60 U.S.
House seats currently listed as “in play” by Inside Elections, an election handicapping website, 38 are in states with Democratic governors.
And while the path to the U.S.
Senate majority does mostly run through red states, and Republicans have, on the whole, not shown much interest in standing up to Trump, it’s not a given that every Republican governor would acquiesce to Trump sending in troops — especially for as norm-shattering a reason as to police an election.
The New York Times also reported this week that multiple Republican politicians privately criticized Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election.
And plenty of sitting Republican governors have had their differences with Trump publicly as well:
- Gov.
Mike DeWine of Ohio (home to three competitive House seats and a pivotal Senate race) is very much an old guard Republican who has objected to Trump’s most controversial behavior.
- Gov.
Kim Reynolds of Iowa (also home to three competitive House seats and a potentially interesting Senate race) endorsed Florida Gov.
Ron DeSantis over Trump in the 2024 Republican presidential primaries and is not running for reelection this year.
- Gov.
Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire (home to two competitive House seats and a vulnerable Democratic-held Senate seat) is a moderate Republican who disavowed Trump in 2016 and waited a conspicuously long time to endorse him in 2024.
- Gov.
Brian Kemp of Georgia (home to another vulnerable Democratic Senate seat) famously rebuffed Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election result in his state.
The Trump administration has thrown cold water all over the idea that it will mobilize the National Guard this November.
A White House spokesperson told NPR in November that concerns about troops at polling places were “baseless conspiracy theories and Democrat talking points.” And in an interview with Vanity Fair late last year, White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles said that “it is categorically false, will not happen.”
But given Trump’s avowed interest in using the National Guard to subvert an election, many officials aren’t taking any chances.
At a conference of local election administrators earlier this month in Virginia, attendees were already gaming out what to do in a scenario where armed troops arrive at a polling place.
Any attempt to use the military to influence the election — even if it’s quickly extinguished by a court — would be one of the most brazen acts of election interference in modern times.
Whether or not it ultimately affected the outcome of the election, it could still shatter many Americans’ belief in the sanctity of the voting booth.
Nathaniel Rakich is Votebeat’s managing editor and is based in Washington, D.C.
Contact Nathaniel at nrakich@votebeat.org.

MARY LOUISE KELLY, HOST:
The election is less than 50 days away, and there is growing concern that President Trump could deploy federalized National Guard troops around polling locations despite clear laws barring such action.
NPR's Kat Lonsdorf reports.
KAT LONSDORF, BYLINE: For months now, a group of several dozen former military lawyers has been writing to Congress with a specific worry - that the U.S.
military might be used in some way to influence the upcoming election.
STEVEN LEPPER: We decided to try to connect the dots that led us to believe that that could be a very real possibility.
LONSDORF: Retired Major General Steven Lepper is part of the nonpartisan Former Judge Advocates Working Group, which has been tracking President Trump's executive orders.
LEPPER: Either this administration is trying to limit the ways in which votes can be cast, or they're setting up a situation where a scenario could be concocted to justify the use of military force.
LONSDORF: He points to the executive order declaring Antifa a domestic terrorist organization.
He says that could potentially be used amid disruption at polling places to justify invoking the Insurrection Act, something Trump has repeatedly threatened to do.
Put in the context of Trump's unprecedented use of the military domestically, particularly his National Guard deployments, Lepper says he and his colleagues see a very clear possible path.
LEPPER: That this administration will ultimately either deploy military forces or paramilitary law enforcement to somehow limit access to polling places.
LONSDORF: The National Guard can legally be used to support elections in many capacities when ordered by state governors.
But the president deploying troops or federal armed agents to polling places is illegal.
It's not just Lepper and his colleagues raising the concern.
In March, several Democratic members of the Senate Armed Services Committee sought assurances from General Gregory Guillot, the commander of USNORTHCOM who would be in charge if such an order came from the president.
When asked by Senator Tammy Duckworth of Illinois what guardrails are in place in that situation, Guillot said he very clearly understands the laws.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
GREGORY GUILLOT: If given the order, I would look at it very closely.
LONSDORF: He said he doesn't think troops should be, quote, "anywhere near polling places." But others have sidestepped such lines of questioning, including the president himself when asked directly about the possibility by reporters in May.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: I'd do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections.
We have to have honest elections.
UNIDENTIFIED REPORTER: So you're not ruling that out?
LONSDORF: NPR asked the White House for clarification on that comment, but did not get a direct response.
In recent weeks, Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan directly pressed several military leaders and federal agencies to confirm that U.S.
troops won't be sent to polling places.
Only chairman of the joint chiefs of staff General Dan Caine has responded, saying that there are, quote, "no plans" to send U.S.
troops to the polls.
There is also growing concern about immigration enforcement agents being used to intimidate voters, something that's also illegal.
Earlier this month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said ICE agents could serve warrants at polling places.
And that, too, could include the military, although that is also considered by most legal experts to be illegal.
An internal DHS memo that was recently made public shows that the administration has outlined a plan specifically to allow for National Guard members to be deputized as immigration enforcement officers, something many members of the administration, like Stephen Miller, have long stated as a goal.
CHIOMA CHUKWU: This memo is designed as a workaround to say, here is how we can get this done without violating federal law.
LONSDORF: Chioma Chukwu is the executive director of American Oversight, a nonpartisan watchdog group that obtained the memo.
The memo, which NPR has read, does not explicitly say anything about elections or polling places.
But Chukwu says, given the administration's escalating claims around voter fraud by unauthorized immigrants...
CHUKWU: We should be planning for this to potentially be the way that they justify deploying National Guard to the polling places around the country.
LONSDORF: DHS told NPR the memo speaks for itself.
Voting officials across the country have been working hard to assure voters there are plans in place if armed federal officials do show up and say they plan on administering the midterms as usual.
Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News, Washington.

The nonpartisan election handicapper the Cook Political Report moved 18 House race ratings toward Democrats on Friday, October 9, 2026, less than four weeks before the November 3, 2026 midterm elections.
The shifts push Cook’s projected outcome to a Democratic net gain of nine to 19 seats, which would give the party between 224 and 234 seats — comfortably above the 218 needed for a majority.
◉ Key Facts
- ►Cook moved 18 House race ratings toward Democrats on Friday, October 9, 2026, roughly 25 days before the November 3, 2026 midterms.
- ►Cook now projects a Democratic net gain of nine to 19 seats, putting the party’s likely House total between 224 and 234 seats — above the 218 needed for control.
- ►Nine Republican incumbents saw their races shift toward Democrats, including Reps.
Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn of Iowa, Ryan Mackenzie, Scott Perry and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Bill Huizenga of Michigan, Rob Wittman of Virginia, French Hill of Arkansas and Victoria Spartz of Indiana.
- ►Five Democratic incumbents — Reps.
Susie Lee (Nev.), Tom Suozzi and Laura Gillen (N.Y.), Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (Wash.) and Don Davis (N.C.) — saw their races tighten further in Democrats’ favor, along with four open seats in Nebraska’s 2nd, Iowa’s 2nd, Kentucky’s 6th and Maine’s 2nd districts.
- ►Cook House editor Erin Covey wrote that Democrats now need to win only about 20% of the Toss Up races to reach a majority, assuming the seats that favor Democrats in Cook’s ratings all break their way.
The Cook Political Report, widely regarded as one of the most closely watched nonpartisan election forecasters in Washington, cited mounting headwinds for Republican candidates tied to the ongoing conflict involving Iran, rising energy prices and broader economic uncertainty.
Cook’s U.S.
House of Representatives editor Erin Covey wrote in her analysis, “With these new moves, we’re also adjusting our range: the most likely outcome is now that Democrats will pick up nine to 19 seats,” adding that “At this point, Democrats only need to win 20 percent of the Toss Ups to get to a majority, assuming the seats that favor Democrats in our ratings all break their way.” Of the races Cook currently classifies as toss-ups, Cook currently labels 21 House contests as “Toss Up,” including 15 Republican-held seats and six Democrat-held districts.
That imbalance means Republicans are defending far more of the most competitive turf than Democrats are, a structural disadvantage that becomes more consequential the longer unfavorable political conditions persist.
The ratings shift arrives despite an aggressive Republican effort to blunt Democratic momentum through advertising.
According to reporting on the shift, Cook Political’s Erin Covey wrote that “In the final weeks of the election, Republicans have hoped that a massive ad campaign effort could dent Democratic candidates’ images and shore up Republicans struggling to free themselves of the anchor of President Donald Trump,” but “With less than four weeks to go, that heavy spending has yet to move the needle.” The scale of the broader shift across forecasters has also drawn attention: according to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, just since Labor Day, Cook Political, Inside Elections, Sabato’s Crystal Ball, and Fox News have made 101 rating changes in Democrats’ favor.
Republicans have pushed back on the characterization that the race is slipping away.
NRCC spokesman Mike Marinella said in a statement that “House races are won in the districts, one by one, with battle-tested candidates and messages that work,” adding that “Pundits in D.C.
can keep guessing, but voters on the ground have a clear contrast between common sense and crazy,” and predicting that “in November, we’re going to win.”

| GOP incumbents shifted toward Democrats | Miller-Meeks & Nunn (Iowa), Mackenzie, Perry & Fitzpatrick (Pa.), Huizenga (Mich.), Wittman (Va.), Hill (Ark.), Spartz (Ind.) |

| Open seats shifted toward Democrats | Nebraska’s 2nd, Iowa’s 2nd, Kentucky’s 6th, Maine’s 2nd |
| New projected House outcome | Democrats: 224-234 seats (net gain of 9-19) |
📚 Background & Context
The Cook Political Report is one of several nonpartisan handicappers, alongside Inside Elections and Sabato’s Crystal Ball, that political strategists, donors and journalists use to gauge the competitiveness of individual House, Senate and gubernatorial races.
The party that does not control the White House has historically gained House seats in midterm elections in most cycles since World War II, a pattern rooted in lower turnout among the president’s supporters and backlash against the incumbent administration’s record.
Rating changes are forecasts based on polling, fundraising, candidate quality and political environment — not predictions of certain outcomes, and Cook and other handicappers routinely revise their ratings again before Election Day as new data emerges.
With roughly three and a half weeks remaining until the November 3, 2026 midterms, both parties are expected to pour additional resources into the newly competitive districts, and further ratings movement from Cook and rival forecasters is likely as early voting begins and more polling is released.
The ultimate test of these projections will come when votes are counted on Election Day, when the accuracy of this cycle’s forecasting models — and the political environment they are attempting to capture — will be fully revealed.
💬 What People Are Saying
Based on public reaction across social media and news platforms, here is the general consensus on this story:
- 🔴Republican voices argue the ratings reflect Washington punditry rather than conditions on the ground, with GOP operatives insisting local candidates and messaging will carry races that national forecasters are writing off prematurely.
- 🔵Democratic strategists and committees are pointing to the shift as validation of a building wave, citing voter anger over the economy and the ongoing Iran conflict as evidence the party is positioned to retake the House majority.
- 🟠Political observers across the spectrum note that while the ratings shift is a meaningful signal, it remains a projection rather than a result, and both parties are bracing for a volatile final stretch before the November 3, 2026 election.

In this era of rampant online gambling, a fitting way to frame this year’s U.S.
House contests is around the odds of Democrats winning a majority.
To put it bluntly, those odds are about as good as anyone can ever expect to find.
But just how many seats will they flip?
The smart money sets the number at around 17.
I’d take the over.
The Democrats start five seats down (219-214), with two vacancies in play—Florida’s 20th District and Texas’ 23rd District.
One of the two is a deep blue constituency, which effectively trims the deficit to four (Texas’ 23rd District is majority Hispanic and supported Trump by 15 points but looks more competitive now).
To regain the gavel, then, the Democrats need just three net wins.
That’s not a big spread to overcome, but the betting card is short, and the GOP does have a couple more cards to play.
To elaborate, district-by-district analysts see 381-395 outcomes as “safely” or “likely” squared away, yielding an effective Republican cushion of seven or eight seats (largely because of its redistricting efforts this year, a point to which I will return).
That leaves only about three or maybe four dozen districts that are truly competitive.
Here’s why I’m wagering that the Democrats will win nearly all of them.
Races and polls
The race-by-race prognosticators are characteristically cautious, anchoring their estimates on district-level factors like partisan balance, incumbency, and candidate quality and discounting national-level dynamics like economic trends and presidential approval.
The theory that politics turns on local issues hasn’t been true for some time; the national trends carry outsized importance now.
As such, some forecasters rely on generic ballot polls, which tally vote intentions for each party without mentioning specific candidates.
They currently favor Democrats by about 6 percentage points, which may not sound seismic, but midterm voters tend to migrate toward the out-party as campaigns progress.
In fact, this century, when an out-party has enjoyed a late-summer lead like this, it has netted between 31 and 63 seats.
That big of a landslide is probably out of reach nowadays (because the number of districts with any semblance of partisan parity has cratered).
Still, those precedents speak to what a 6-point lead really represents.
Presidential patterns
We can reach the same conclusion, though, without even looking at election polls.
It is something close to an ironclad law that the president’s party loses seats in midterm elections—typically more than two dozen of them.
In fact, in only three such elections since the Civil War has the president’s party not lost seats: 1934 (reflecting New Deal optimism), 2002 (rallying post-9/11 patriotism), and 1998 (responding to perceived impeachment overreach).
What did those years have in common?
A remarkably popular president.
Clinton’s approval stood at 66%.
Bush’s stood at 63%.
And though FDR’s is less clear because scientific polling had yet to be invented, the robust economic rebound of that year connotes broad public support.
Indeed, by contrast, when a president’s approval rating is underwater, his seat loss spikes substantially.
Because Trump’s approval (mid/high 30’s) is among the lowest of any president at this point in his term since 1946—when Truman’s Democrats lost 55 seats—history portends an uphill battle.
And with gas prices and mortgage rates both up, job growth and consumer confidence both down, and Iran tensions and ICE shootings both unabated, Trump’s numbers are unlikely to rebound anytime soon—certainly not before voting begins in two-to-six weeks.
Truth be told, Trump is probably even less popular than previous presidents were with similar ratings.
While dissatisfied Democrats are willing to voice that discontent on surveys, modern-day Republicans tend to “cheerlead” and loathe to give pollsters the supposed satisfaction of hearing their disapproval.
But their enthusiasm may still be waning, and there’s no guarantee they’ll cast ballots for down-ballot Republicans.
Thus, the projected seat loss from Trump’s unpopularity may be lowballing it.
A big part of the presidential party’s midterm seat loss is about turnout.
Unpopular presidents tend to dampen enthusiasm among supporters and boost it among opponents.
In Trump’s case, it applies even when he is more popular; the “cult of personality” nature of his appeal draws supporters out of the woodwork when he’s on the ballot but not when he isn’t.
Equally important to the turnout story—and often overlooked among pundits—is the “diploma divide” that has realigned the two parties’ class identities.
That upheaval has taken Democrats, as Paul Begala said, “from the factory floor to the faculty lounge,” but it has also taken them to the ballot box.
In other words, because (a) education is such a powerful predictor of voting, and (b) Democrats have become the ones who tend to have more of it, they (c) tend to have a turnout advantage in low-visibility elections (non-presidential years) now.
What about …
There are several objections to consider, of course.
First, what about the 2022 midterms, when Democrats performed well despite Biden’s unpopularity?
Well, while the Democrats did gain a seat in the Senate, the party still lost nine seats in the House—three times what Republicans can afford this year.
And as I mentioned earlier, Biden’s number then did not mean the same thing that Trump’s does now.
A meaningful share of Biden’s disapprovers were frustrated Democrats who were never going to vote red.
By contrast, relatively few of Trump’s disapprovers are Republican voters, making his disapproval rating more consequential.
But what about the systematic survey bias in favor of Democrats?
Swing-state polls overestimated Democratic support in 2016, 2020, and 2024, so why shouldn’t we take the Democrats’ current polling lead with a grain of salt?
Because the pattern did not hold in either of the last two midterms: 2018 and 2022 were both relatively accurate polling years; if anything, the 2022 polls underestimated the Democrats’ showing.
So, what about all the radicals the Democrats have been nominating who stand stiff odds of winning over swing voters?
That narrative doesn’t hold up; leftist victories have received outsized media attention, but just as many centrists have been winning overall, and in the real House battlegrounds, Democratic primary voters have mostly stuck to mainstream candidates.
Even the so-called radicals are not necessarily unelectable.
Their leftist rhetoric is usually concentrated on economic issues—reflecting a rising tide of populism among not just Democrats but independents and Republicans as well.
Well, what about the fundraising advantage that Republicans enjoy?
Republican Party committees and allied groups currently hold a half-billion-dollar cash edge over their Democratic counterparts.
But that top-line gap doesn’t show up where it matters most: In the second quarter of 2026, Democratic challengers outraised Republican incumbents in about two-thirds of the toss-up districts.
And even where a real gap does exist, money has diminishing returns; candidates need enough cash to get their message out, but beyond that, those additional millions buy less and less.
Finally, what about the Republicans’ new gerrymanders?
Indeed, those mid-cycle redistricting gambits have genuinely hurt Democrats; the median district is about two points more Republican than it was before they redrew the maps.
But that damage is already baked into the competitive-seat math that I laid out at the beginning.
It’s the reason that Democrats will not gain 50 seats.
They are in a pretty good position to gain around 25-30, though, which would amount to a decisive rebuke of the Trump sequel and his many foot soldiers on Capitol Hill.

The midterm elections are 100 days out.
Political reporter Hans Nichols, lead author of the Hill Leaders newsletter, shares his intel on the state of the races:
The big picture: The House environment favors the Democrats.
The terrain favors Republicans.
The same is broadly true on the Senate side — except the structural advantages are even greater for Republicans.
THE HOUSE — currently 218 Rs, 212 Ds, 1 independent, and 4 vacancies
Why Democrats are upbeat
The polls.
The latest Fox News poll has Democrats ahead by 7 points on the generic ballot.
Toss in Democratic enthusiasm — and the fact that Democratic candidates have outperformed 2024 nominee Kamala Harris in the vast majority of special elections — and you can see why House Republicans are privately so nervous.
The cost of living.
Yes, inflation has cooled.
But prices have risen during the first two years of President Trump's current term, and that's especially true on the one billboard everyone sees — gas prices.
The real political gift for Democrats is the direct link between $4-a-gallon gasoline and the unpopular war in Iran that Trump launched.
Why Republicans are cautiously optimistic
Redistricting.
Add up all the mid-cycle redistricting in nine states, squint through a Republican lens, and you'll see nine new GOP seats.
Put on Democratic glasses and assume that Republicans are renting a few of those seats (especially in mostly Hispanic parts of the Rio Grande Valley) instead of owning them, and it looks closer to six seats.
Either way, Republicans like where they ended up in the redistricting wars of 2026.
There are now 23 Democrats running for the House in districts Trump carried in 2024 — vs.
eight Republicans who represent districts Harris won (half are in California).
One key battleground
For House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), the road to the majority runs through Iowa, which has been hit hard by inflation (think fertilizer as much as diesel) and retaliatory agriculture tariffs.
In 2018, Democrats picked up two of the three seats the GOP held.
On a good night this year, they'd pick up two of the current four Republican seats.
Three for four would be a great night.
But if Republicans hold all four of those seats, it's hard to see a Democrat winning the gavel.
THE SENATE — currently 53 Rs, 45 Ds, and 2 independents who caucus with Ds
Why Republicans are upbeat
The national environment is grim, but every state is its own ecosystem and the map favors Republicans.
Democrats need to flip four seats, including at least two in solidly red states.
Maine.
Give Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) credit.
He recruited his way out of a bad map.
But he didn't run the table, and in Maine his worst nightmare came true: Democrats have an untested candidate against a proven winner.
After populist Democrat Graham Platner flamed out (predictably, Schumer would tell you), Republicans are about to unload on the new substitute nominee, Troy Jackson.
Meanwhile, incumbent GOP Sen.
Susan Collins is well-funded and ready to make her case that she delivers for Maine as appropriations chair — shipbuilding, rural hospitals, firehouses.
If Democrats lose Maine, they'll need to win in three double-digit Trump states.
Schumer loves a pair of recruits in two such red states because they've won statewide before: former Sen.
Sherrod Brown in Ohio and former Rep.
Mary Peltola in Alaska.
Then Democrats will need some magic in Texas or Iowa — or both, if Democrats lose Michigan.
This brings us to the final wildcard of the Democratic primary season: the Aug.
4 showdown between Rep.
Haley Stevens and progressive insurgent Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.
Stevens' money advantage is staggering — $50 million to $1 million on the PAC front in the last two months.
And yet the race is tiedin the polls.
Many establishment Democrats think El-Sayed — who has the support of progressive Rep.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) — is too far left to win a general election.
El-Sayed's run for Senate is something of a proving ground for AOC, who's weighing a bid for Senate or president in 2028.

Syria, Israel hold US-mediated talks in Jordan to de-escalate tensions
Syria’s foreign minister meets with an Israeli delegation led by the chief of the Mossad to de-escalate tensions after an Israeli strike near the Turkish border.
Syria’s Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani has met with Israeli intelligence officials in Jordan, according to Syrian state media, as the two sides work to de-escalate tensions following an Israeli attack on a Syrian airbase near the Turkish border.
Syria’s Sana news agency, citing a diplomatic source, said the talks were mediated by the United States and involved a “high-level Israeli delegation”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Israel bombs Syria as US envoy says base attack aimed at ‘baiting’ Turkiye
- list 2 of 3Envoy says Israel did not give the US notice before strikes on Syrian base
- list 3 of 3Syria’s foreign minister says door open for diplomacy with Israel
The AFP news agency reported that al-Shaibani met the head of Israel’s Mossad intelligence agency, Roman Gofman.
According to Sana, the discussions “focused on establishing practical mechanisms to halt Israeli attacks, arrests and targeting operations” as well as “reviving negotiations for a lasting security agreement between the two sides”.
They also discussed efforts to ease tensions between Israel and Turkiye and to prevent their rivalry from spilling onto Syrian territory, Sana reported.
The US has sought to broker a security agreement between Israel and the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa for more than a year.
Israel has launched hundreds of strikes on Syria since the fall of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024 and sent troops into a United Nations-patrolled buffer zone that had long separated Israeli and Syrian forces in the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights.
It also bombed the Abu Duhur airbase in northwestern Idlib on Thursday, claiming the attack was to prevent Turkish troops from deploying at the base, a claim Syria and Turkiye have denied.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have also traded barbs since the incident, with tensions high between the two leaders.
According to Sana, the Syrian side stressed during Sunday’s talks “that Syria is a sovereign state with the full right to rebuild and develop its national army and determine its alliances and partnerships in line with its national interests”.
The Syrian side rejected “any arrangements or mechanisms that would restrict these sovereign rights,” it said.
Syria’s immediate priorities in the talks remained an Israeli withdrawal to positions held before al-Assad’s overthrow and the full restoration of a 1974 disengagement agreement, Sana reported.
The Syrian officials also reaffirmed Damascus’s sovereignty over the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights, it added.
Israel’s ‘red lines’
Israeli media reported that the talks were “positive” and said Israeli officials had adopted a number of red lines going into talks.
These include preventing Turkish military activity in Syria, keeping the Syrian side of the Golan Heights demilitarised, “ensuring the security” of Syria’s Druze community and preventing the Syrian army from acquiring certain strategic weapons systems.
They also conditioned any withdrawal from Syrian territories occupied by Israel on “diplomatic achievements”.
During previous rounds of US-mediated talks, Syria and Israel had agreed on a joint mechanism to share intelligence and defuse tensions.
But the negotiations froze at the end of February, when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran, without a date set for resumption.
In an interview published ahead of the meeting, al-Shaibani told Reuters news agency that Damascus did not trust Israel, but that the door remained open for diplomacy.
He said Syria had cut off contact entirely after the Israeli attack on Syria’s Abu al-Duhur airbase last week.
Al-Shaibani said the two sides had agreed on paper to “almost everything” around the beginning of the year, including arrangements for security zones in southern Syria and a buffer zone where only UN forces would be present.
Hassan Mneimneh, a political analyst and researcher at the Middle East Institute, told Al Jazeera that the current round of talks was unlikely to de-escalate tensions given Israel’s track record.
“It’s quite the opposite, meaning now that Syria has indicated its desire to have the situation de-escalate, Israel is likely to bring in more demands and have the Americans basically negotiate these new demands with Syria, against any kind of expansion of Turkish presence in the north and beyond the north,” he said.
Mneimneh added that Syria was “afraid that the country will become a battlefield” between Israel and Turkiye and was concerned about Israel’s territorial grab in the country, stretching “all the way to Hermon, to Jabal al-Sheikh in its totality almost, and all the way to three southern provinces”.
So, from the Syrian perspective, Mneimneh added, the talks with Israel seem to be aimed at avoiding “the disintegration of Syrian authority” as well as ensuring any conflict between Israel and Turkiye does not prevent Syria from “forming, establishing, consolidating polity after the fall of” al-Assad.

Protests took place in Syria on October 23 as Syrians condemned “Israeli incursions and attacks,” according to Syrian state media.
The protests came a day after Syrians claimed an unarmed civilian was killed in an Israeli raid near the border.
The Israeli military has not commented on the incident.
The demonstrations also occurred amid a flurry of diplomatic activity by Syrian officials, including a meeting between Syria’s President Ahmed al Sharaa and US Envoy Tom Barrack in Damascus.
The protests followed an October 18 statement by Syria’s Foreign Ministry condemning Israeli military incursions into southern Syria.
Israel took control of a buffer zone along the Golan border with Syria on December 8, 2024, when the Bashar al Assad regime fell.
Israel also seized the peak of Mount Hermon.
In the intervening year and 10 months, Israeli officials have said they will not leave the buffer zone as long as threats from Syria remain.
Israel’s policy along the border with Syria is part of a broader strategy that has emerged since Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023.
On October 18, 2026, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu noted that Israel’s national security doctrine has shifted to “giving priority to prevention and offense over containment and defense.” As part of the doctrine in Syria, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) has established new positions in the buffer zone that runs along the 1974 ceasefire line.
The IDF has also carried out raids into Syria to detain suspects and dismantle “terrorist infrastructure.”
During one such operation on October 22, Israeli soldiers shot and killed a Syrian man with disabilities in the village of Jamla, according to Syrian state media.
The village lies about half a mile from the Bravo Line, the Syrian boundary of a buffer zone established under the 1974 disengagement agreement between Israel and Syria.
The Alpha Line marks the Israeli side of the zone.
Before December 8, 2024, Israeli forces remained largely west of the Alpha Line, but they have since entered the buffer zone and expanded operations beyond the Bravo Line.
The IDF does not comment often on these operations, but it said on October 5 that it had detained two suspects in Syria.
On October 22, Syria’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the IDF operation.
It added that Syria holds Israel responsible for the man’s death, “stressing that ongoing incursions and attacks against Syrian citizens violate the sovereignty of the Syrian Arab Republic, threaten regional security and stability, and hinder recovery and reconstruction efforts.” The next day, protests were held in the country.
“In Quneitra, hundreds of men, women and children took part in a protest condemning Israeli aggressions and reaffirming Syria’s territorial unity,” the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) said.
Quneitra is near the Golan border with Israel.
Protests also occurred in Syria’s southern Daraa province and in Damascus.
Syria has called on the international community to help end Israeli operations.
Syrian officials also held a number of meetings with partners in the region on October 21 and 22.
On October 22, Jordan’s King Abdullah II hosted Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al Shaibani, during which Shaibani discussed Israel’s “attacks” in southern Syria.
Abdullah previously criticized Israel’s role in Syria in a speech at the United Nations General Assembly in September.
On October 22, Shaibani held a phone call with United Arab Emirates Minister of Foreign Affairs Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
Syrian officials provided only general details about the call.
Syrian President Ahmad al Sharaa met US Special Presidential Envoy for Syria and Iraq Tom Barrack in Damascus on October 23.
“The two sides discussed cooperation aimed at advancing both countries’ interests and strengthening security and stability,” SANA reported.
Barrack, who is also the US ambassador to Turkey, described the meeting as productive and added that “Syria plays a pivotal role in securing lasting peace—its destiny touches every face of the Middle East’s Rubik’s Cube.”
polymarket-4096541.title: Protests break out in Syria against 'Israeli incursions and attacks' as tensions rise

polymarket-4096541.text:
Syria sharpened its criticism of Israeli military operations in Syria during the first week of October, including the construction of a new fortified security line in southern Syria, east of the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights.
On October 6, in one of several recent statements from Damascus, Syria’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations Ibrahim Olabi condemned Israel for “violations of international law and human rights” in actions near the Golan.
It is one of several recent statements from Damascus, and several regional countries have joined Syria in its condemnations.
At the same time, Syria conducted outreach to Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE and condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) noted on October 6 that Olabi “stressed the need to hold Israel accountable for its violations of international law and human rights, reaffirming that the Golan will remain Syrian territory and that all Israeli measures aimed at annexing it are null and void under international law and U.N.
Security Council Resolution 497.”
The comments come in the context of Israel’s operations in Syria in the wake of the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) moved into the buffer zone that previously separated Israel and Syrian forces since 1974 and took the peak of Mount Hermon.
Israeli officials, particularly the Defense Minister Israel Katz, have repeatedly said they will not leave the new buffer zone along the old border as long as jihadist threats persist.
Syria is concerned that Israel is establishing a new permanent presence in Syria.
On October 4, Syria’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned Israel for extending its control to a new line called the “Sufa 53 line.” SANA noted that the ministry “called on the international community to assume its responsibilities and take effective deterrent measures to put an end to these violations and prevent their recurrence.” Qatar and Jordan joined in the condemnation with statements on October 4.
On October 5, Turkey also condemned Israel’s moves regarding the Sufa 53 line.
The statements appear coordinated.
Israel hasn’t commented on the Syrian statements.
However, on October 7, as part of the IDF’s statements about three years of war since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, the Israeli military released new details about its role in Syria.
It noted that in the wake of the fall of the Assad regime, the IDF’s “210th Division entered Syrian territory and began establishing a forward security area, within which ten military posts were established.”
Syria also continued its diplomatic outreach in early October.
US Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack, who is also US envoy to Syria and Iraq, met with Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al Shaibani in Turkey on October 8.
“Syria is a key component of the Middle East Rubik’s Cube and is assisting the region in finding an algorithm to lower the temperatures in its neighborhood,” Barrack noted.
“Pleased to meet with Syrian Foreign Minister al-Shaibani today to discuss our shared priorities in addressing regional threats,” he added.
Syria also condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as Pakistan and Turkey increased support for Riyadh amid the conflict in Yemen.
In addition, on October 7, Syria’s president spoke with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
“The two sides … explored ways to boost economic and investment cooperation and expand partnerships between the two countries, stressing the importance of continuing coordination and communication on issues of common interest,” SANA reported.
Syria has experienced success in its diplomatic outreach since the fall of the Assad regime.
Saudi Arabia and Turkey remain its key partners in the region, and early October calls and meetings reflected this trend.
Syrian President Ahmed al Sharaa visited Saudi Arabia to meet with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on October 6, and Syria’s foreign minister met his Turkish counterpart on October 7, after meeting the US envoy.

military forces in the Middle East could launch major operations against Iran within 96 hours of receiving an order from President Donald Trump, according to reports, as senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Tehran to discuss regional security and de-escalating tensions.

Iran calls for 'single force' among Islamic nations at major summit on Mideast tensions
Officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Tehran on Monday in a bid to de-escalate Middle East tensions.
The leaders focused on "Islamic unity, regional security & standing against US-backed Israeli aggression," the Iranian government said in a post on X.
The meeting also marked the first high-level engagement between Iran and the three signatories to August's Mecca mutual defense pact.
During the talks with Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani Army Chief Gen.
Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief İbrahim Kalın, Pezeshkian urged Islamic nations to act as "a single force," with Tehran framing the summit around regional security, Islamic solidarity and resistance to U.S.-backed Israeli actions.
According to Reuters, Saudi Arabia also said the visit was intended to open negotiating channels to "prevent the return of military escalation."
General Mohsen Rezaei, the Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, hosted Monday's meeting.
Guterres demands new Middle East security framework, warns against interference
U.N.
Secretary-General António Guterres called for a fundamental overhaul of Middle Eastern diplomacy on Monday, urging regional powers to build a “new security architecture.”
“No country in the Middle East can achieve lasting security at the expense of another,” Guterres wrote on X, calling for a new regional framework.
“One in which the future is shaped by the peoples & countries of the region, rather than by war after war after war – many times fueled by external actors,” he said.
Saudi Arabia thwarts Houthi missile barrage amid escalating conflict
The Saudi-led coalition shot down three ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis toward the Eastern Province on Monday, thwarting a fresh cross-border assault as hostilities between the two sides escalated.
“Air defenses intercepted and destroyed 3 ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the eastern region,” Saudi military spokesman Col.
Turki al-Malki said in a post on X.
Earlier, Saudi Civil Defense issued warnings of a potential hostile threat in the Eastern Province and Al-Kharj, before later saying the danger had passed in both areas.
Trump reveals why he never liked Iran cease-fire: 'Waste of time'
President Donald Trump declared Monday that past ceasefires with Iran were ineffective, brushing aside previous efforts to de-escalate tensions with Iran.
“We did a little cease-fire, which I never liked very much,” he said of the April arrangement.
“I considered it sort of a waste of time,” he added.
“But, you know, you like to listen to professionals,” Trump said at a rally in Mississippi.
“But we did a little cease-fire, so we let some ships get in.”
“You know, we want to be nice, but it was just a waste of time as far as I'm concerned.”
“But, we're doing a job.
We're doing a job for you,” Trump added.
The U.S.-Iran ceasefire took effect in April following its initial announcement.
It was later formalized and extended under the 60-day Islamabad Memorandum signed in June before collapsing in July.
Trump says Iran 'started the war,' claims America had 'no choice' but to fight
President Donald Trump said Monday that Iran was responsible for starting the war between the two countries.
“We didn’t start the war with Iran.
Iran started the war with us,” Trump said Monday at a campaign rally in Mississippi and pointed to Iran’s history of hostile actions against the United States dating back to 1979.
Trump also said Iranian leaders were just two weeks away from developing a nuclear missile and described them as “very smart people.”
“But we've beat the sh**t out of them.
And I don't feel we had a choice.
“They were two weeks away from having a nuclear missile.
They're considered the number one state sponsor of terror in the world,” the president added.
Hezbollah prepares for new regional war with Iran funds: report
Hezbollah has spent three months preparing for the possibility of a new war with Israel after receiving funds from Iran, Lebanese security personnel told Reuters.
The focus, the officials said, was on procuring explosives and producing drones that can be flown into Israeli positions.
Hezbollah had received tens of millions of dollars from Iran to help boost its military capabilities, the sources said.
Hezbollah's media office also said that Israel's occupation of Lebanese land made any resistance to it a legitimate right.
Hostilities had eased over the summer as an interim U.S.-Iran deal included a ceasefire in Lebanon, and as Washington mediated talks between Lebanon and Israel.
Trump brands Soleimani 'father of the roadside bomb,' blasts Iran for maiming US troops
President Donald Trump blasted Iran and the late Qasem Soleimani on Monday, blaming Tehran for decades of American casualties caused by sophisticated roadside bombs.
“In 1979, and they were killing our people for years,” Trump said at a rally in Mississippi.
“A lot of people died individually with the roadside bombs,” he added.
“Soleimani.
You know, Soleimani.
I killed him in my first term.
Soleimani.
“You know, we have people all over the country with no legs or with no arms, with a face that's been destroyed, young, beautiful people.
“Soleimani was the father of the roadside bomb.
And our guys were getting really good at detecting them.
So they started making them more powerful and all out of plastic," he said.
“They're made out of plastic and so the metal detectors don't work," Trump explained before adding, "That was done by Iran because they made those bombs.
They made all of the roadside bombs."
“They gave them out.
It was Soleimani's favorite weapon,” Trump said.
“And I heard you, Congressman, get up and say about 1979, that's absolutely true.
“It was.
They've been killing our people and other people too,” the president said.

U.S.
Central Command highlighted ongoing flight operations aboard the USS George Washington on Monday, sharing footage of flight deck crew refueling jets in the Arabian Sea.
"U.S.
Sailors refuel aircraft during flight operations aboard USS George Washington (CVN 73)," CENTCOM said on X.
"Every military mission success begins and ends with people," it added.
The supercarrier is currently deployed in the Arabian Sea within the U.S.
5th Fleet's and CENTCOM's areas of responsibility.

Iran's armed forces chief of staff, Maj.
Gen.
Ali Abdollahi, issued a warning to shipping companies Monday, stating that any ship violating the country's security protocols in the southern waters of the Strait of Hormuz is at risk.
“Any vessel that attempts to deviate from the designated route or disregard Iranian procedures, for any reason, will put itself at risk and face serious damage,” Abdollahi said, according to the state-run Islamic Republic News Agency (IRNA).

La junta directiva del Banco de la República anunció la decisión sobre la tasa de interés.
Luego de varios encuentros con la tasa congelada, en esta oportunidad hubo mayorías para un incremento.
Publicado por: Redacción Vanguardia
La junta directiva del Banco de la República decidió aumentar la tasa de interés en 25 puntos básicos (pbs) durante la reunión de este 30 de septiembre.
Esta determinación rompe la tendencia de mantener inalterada la tasa de interés en los últimos encuentros.
Esta es la primera decisión en la que participa el gobierno de Abelardo De La Espriella, representado por el ministro de Hacienda, Miguel Gómez.
De acuerdo con el gerente general del Banco de la República, Leonardo Villar Gómez, explicó que este aumento corresponde a un paso más del ajuste de la política monetaria.
El gerente del Emisor recalcó que la inflación (6,24 %) se encuentra aún distante de la meta del 3 %.
En esta oportunidad, cuatro codirectores votaron por el incremento de 25 (pbs), mientras que dos votaron por mantenerla inalterado.
Un solo codirector votó por un ajuste de 50 (pbs).
En la última encuesta de ANIF, 16 de 22 analistas consultados anticipaban que las tasas se mantendrían inalteradas en este encuentro.
Solo dos anticipaban un aumento de 25 puntos básicos y cuatro veían un incremento de 50 pbs.
En su intervención, el gerente general del Emisor recordó que la determinación de aumentar la tasa de interés mantiene una “política monetaria restrictiva”, que va de la mano con una intención de reducir la inflación en 2027.
“La información futura sobre los efectos del fenómeno de El Niño, el proceso de recuperación después del terremoto, y las medidas de política fiscal, serán importantes para las próximas decisiones de política monetaria”, agregó el gerente Villar.
Publicidad
¿Por qué es importante la tasa de interés?
La tasa de interés es clave para el crecimiento económico, como para el control de la inflación.
Este es el valor mínimo que le cobra el Banco de la República a las entidades financieras por la liquidez que les suministra.
Cuando sube la tasa, se encarece el costo del crédito, lo que puede reducir el gasto de los consumidores.
Aunque el efecto no se traslada inmediatamente al bolsillo de los colombianos,es la referencia que tiene todo el sistema financiero para las tasas de interés.

Grupo Cibest Expects Colombia to Raise Rates to 12.50% and the Fed to Hold
Two Rate Decisions, Two Days Apart: Same Direction, Different Pace
Colombia’s central bank, the Banco de la República (Bank of the Republic), would raise its policy rate by 25 basis points on October 30, from 12.25% to 12.50%, while the US Federal Reserve would hold its own rate at 3.75% to 4.00% two days earlier, on October 28.
Those are the central expectations set out in the October 26 editorial of Radar Bancolombia, the weekly macroeconomic and markets report from Bancolombia, the Colombian banking subsidiary of Grupo Cibest (NYSE: CIB; BVC: CIBEST, PFCIBEST).
Both central banks raised rates in September, which Grupo Cibest said was the first time since 2023 that the two had moved in the same direction, and the bank expects both to raise again in December.
What separates them this week, the report said, is pace rather than direction.
Both face inflation that is not receding, but the sources differ: in the United States, energy prices tied to the conflict in the Middle East are keeping inflation above target, while in Colombia the pressure comes from the persistence of indexation mechanisms and from supply shocks to food associated with El Niño.
That difference, the report said, would define how much room each authority has.
The editorial, Decisiones de política monetaria: mismo rumbo, distinto ritmo (Monetary Policy Decisions: Same Direction, Different Pace), was written by Valentina Guáqueta, an inflation and central banking analyst, and edited by José Luis Mojica, macroeconomic manager, and Laura Clavijo, director of the bank’s Dirección de Investigaciones Económicas, Sectoriales y de Mercado (Economic, Sector and Market Research Department).
Quotations from the report are Finance Colombia translations from the Spanish.
“The discussion in Colombia would not be when the cuts would begin, but how long a sufficiently restrictive stance must be maintained.” — Valentina Guáqueta, inflation and central banking analyst, Bancolombia
Colombian Inflation Reached 6.29% in September
The expectation of a further 25 basis point increase rests on an inflation picture that continues to deteriorate, with pressure concentrated in the most persistent components of the basket and in those most exposed to supply shocks, according to the report.
Annual inflation accelerated to 6.29% in September, its highest level since July 2024.
Services inflation stood at 7.19%, which the report attributed to the fact that a good part of its prices reset on the basis of past inflation or the minimum wage increase, and perishable foods, whose annual variation reached 14.14%, added to that in the face of supply shocks associated with El Niño.
Finance Colombia reported the full September breakdown on October 12, and Grupo Cibest’s economists set out the case for a 7.3% peak in 2027 earlier this month.
Analysts’ expectations for the close of 2026 stand at 6.83%, more than double the 3% target, and their expectations for 2027 have risen without interruption in recent months, the report said.
None of the fronts the board of directors identified as determining factors points to relief: El Niño would extend into the second quarter of 2027, and the fiscal adjustment has not yet been defined.
The Board’s September Vote Narrowed to Two for a Hold
The report said the persistence of those pressures has gained weight inside the board, pointing to its September vote and the minutes of that meeting.
The option of leaving the rate unchanged went from four votes in July to only two.
The minutes also noted that, for most of its members, inflationary pressures have stopped being concentrated in isolated shocks and have spread to a larger share of the basket.
Grupo Cibest anticipates the board would approve the increase by majority, with a vote that would remain divided.
Activity Contracted in the Earthquake Month
The loss of momentum in economic activity would be a new element in the discussion, though not enough to interrupt the cycle, the report said.
The Indicador de Seguimiento a la Economía (Economic Monitoring Indicator, ISE) contracted 0.04% on an annual basis in August, below Grupo Cibest’s own expectation of 0.3% growth and largely a reflection of the damage caused by the August 10 earthquake.
Primary and secondary activities fell 3.2% and 3.0%, with the result in the first case possibly explained by weak performance in agriculture and a negative contribution from manufacturing, alongside still-lagging construction, in the second.
Tertiary activities limited the fall, growing 1.1% with increases in five of the seven macro-sectors, though public administration and recreation expanded only 2.2% against an average of 7.1% over the first seven months of the year.
The report said the figure would strengthen the position of the two co-directors who voted to hold the rate, but added that part of the shock would be transitory and that activity is still growing 2.27% so far this year.
Grupo Cibest Sees Both Rates Ending the Year Higher
Beyond this week’s decisions, Grupo Cibest said attention would center on the signals both central banks give about the path of rates.
In the bank’s scenario, each would close the year with one final increase in December, taking Colombia’s policy rate to 12.75% and the federal funds rate to a range of 4.00% to 4.25%.
The report said risks remain skewed to the upside: a more intense El Niño, a prolongation of the Middle East conflict or a significant increase in the minimum wage could all extend the cycle.
A Fed pause would not modify the bank’s Colombian scenario, though the report said it would ease external pressures, since a wider rate differential would favor the peso and help contain the prices of imported goods.
Finance Colombia reported earlier this month on the bank’s view that higher Fed rates would limit the room for a cheaper dollar in Colombia, and on the September decisions that opened this phase of the cycle.
US Payroll Growth Slowed to 29,000 in September
The Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously in September to raise the federal funds target range by 25 basis points, to 3.75% to 4.00%.
Grupo Cibest noted that it was the first increase since July 2023 and put the rate at its highest level since November 2025.
Since then, the report said, the committee’s discussion has stopped turning on whether further increases are needed and has concentrated on when they would be delivered.
The behavior of the labor market would be decisive in setting that moment, and its moderation would remove the urgency of a new increase, because employment has stopped being a source of pressure on prices.
Nonfarm payrolls grew by 29,000 in September, far below expectations, and wage growth slowed to 3.0%, the weakest pace in five years.
Even so, the report described the labor market as showing no deterioration: the unemployment rate has held between 4.1% and 4.3% since March, and jobless claims remain below 200,000.
That moderation, combined with PCE inflation of 3.42% in August against an expected 3.7%, pushed the market to shift the increase it had anticipated for October into December, according to the report.
September’s consumer price index, higher than forecast, briefly lifted the probability of an increase at this week’s meeting to near 50%, the report said, but that probability fell back after several committee members dismissed the urgency of a new move.
As of the close on Friday, October 23, the market assigned a probability near 90.6% to rates staying unchanged and 69.1% to a 25 basis point increase in December.
US Inflation Accelerated to 3.7% on Energy Prices
A pause would not mean the end of the cycle, the report said.
Consumer price inflation accelerated to 3.7% in September, driven by energy, whose annual inflation stands at 20.4%, with gasoline alone accounting for more than half the monthly rise in the index.

ADEN — Houthi forces have occupied Mayyun Island — the 13-square-kilometre volcanic outcrop that divides the Bab el-Mandeb Strait into two shipping channels — since 11 September 2026, and no military operation has targeted the island itself.
The only attempt to reverse the Houthis’ hold on the strait is Operation Dawn of Yemen, a coalition ground offensive launched on 4 October and focused on the mainland coast.
For more on this, see Lloyd’s war risk premiums on Hormuz transits.
Cargo transits through the strait stood at 1,215 vessels in September, 47 percent below pre-crisis levels, according to Lloyd’s List Intelligence.
The Strait of Hormuz dominates Western headlines, but the ground-level occupation of Bab el-Mandeb — through which an estimated 12 percent of global seaborne trade passes — has drawn almost no sustained editorial attention from Reuters, Bloomberg, or the Financial Times.
Two simultaneously contested chokepoints have compressed the economics of every cargo moving between Asia and Europe: Hormuz, where Iran’s state actors operate, and Bab el-Mandeb, where a non-state force now holds the island commanding the strait itself.

How Did Houthi Forces Reach Mayyun Island?
Houthi fighters crossed to Mayyun — also called Perim Island — by boat on 11 September 2026, following government forces’ withdrawal.
The advance came hours after Houthi forces took the port city of Mocha on the mainland coast, removing the last government-held position on Yemen’s southern Red Sea coastline.
Both events were confirmed by a senior Yemeni government military official and a Houthi official, both speaking to the Associated Press (Al Jazeera, 2026-09-12; Euronews, 2026-09-12).
The seizure followed the fall of Mocha on the mainland coast, which Houthi forces captured as government troops retreated toward the town of Dhubab.
The collapse was rapid.
Mocha was the last government-held position on Yemen’s southern Red Sea coast.
By the morning of 11 September, Houthi forces had crossed the water to the island.
The Houthis also claimed control of the Greater and Lesser Hanish Islands further north in the Red Sea, though this rests on a single AFP-cited military official and has not been independently corroborated (Al Jazeera, 2026-09-12).
The advance had been building through the summer.
The 2022 Yemen truce formally collapsed in July 2026, according to the BBC (2026-10-11), and the Houthis pressed south through government-held territory along the Red Sea coast.
The offensive cost more than 500 lives and displaced approximately 46,000 people before the government counter-offensive began, according to the International Organization for Migration (Times of Israel/IOM, 2026-09-12).
Mocha and Mayyun fell in the final 48 hours of that push.
Security analyst Wolfgang Pusztai told Al Jazeera that the Houthis’ new position gives them “the capability to shut down maritime traffic through Bab al-Mandeb” and allows the use of “shorter-range missiles instead of long-range artillery” (Al Jazeera, 2026-09-12).
The shift from long-range harassment to close-range territorial control changed the nature of the threat: a missile fired from Mayyun has a shorter flight time, a lower intercept window, and requires less logistical support than one launched from the Yemeni highlands.
Dr.
Andreas Krieg of King’s College London assessed that the group is “well placed to hold [Mayyun] in the short term because they control the surrounding areas,” but that the island would be difficult to defend against an amphibious assault over the longer term.
“The key is holding the coastal mainland and its hinterland,” Krieg said (Al Jazeera, 2026-09-12).
What Does Mayyun’s Position Mean for Red Sea Shipping?
Mayyun sits at the narrowest point of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which measures 18 miles across at its tightest, according to the US Energy Information Administration.
Any vessel transiting must pass within range of territory now controlled by the Houthis, who hold both the island and Yemen’s entire Red Sea coastline to its north and east.
The island divides the passage into two channels — giving a territorial occupier firing positions on both.
Before the Red Sea crisis began in November 2023, approximately 9.3 million barrels of oil per day transited the strait, the EIA estimated.
By 2025, that flow had fallen to approximately 4.1 to 4.2 million barrels per day, according to an IEA estimate reported by Montel (2026-07-21).
The strait also carries an estimated 8 percent of the world’s liquefied natural gas (Al Jazeera, 2026-09-12).

The September transit data complicates a simple narrative of decline following the Mayyun seizure.
The Lloyd’s List figures show transits 4 percent higher than August and 16 percent above the same month a year earlier, even as they remained nearly half the pre-crisis baseline.
The long-term depression predates the island’s fall — it began with Houthi attacks on commercial shipping in November 2023 — and the seizure has not yet produced a measurable further drop.
What it has done, in the assessment of analysts Pusztai and Krieg, is give the Houthis the physical infrastructure to enforce a full closure should they choose to.
A closure of Bab el-Mandeb would force tankers from the Persian Gulf to reroute around the southern tip of Africa, according to the EIA.
A container ship taking the Cape of Good Hope route adds roughly three weeks to a round trip between the Gulf and northern Europe, substantially increasing fuel and time costs.
The rerouting wave is already well established since 2024, but the physical occupation of Mayyun raises the question of whether the remaining traffic — vessels whose operators judged the risk acceptable at earlier insurance rates — will continue to transit as premiums and threat assessments adjust.
The Cost to Global Trade
War-risk insurance premiums for Red Sea transits roughly doubled in August 2026 to approximately 1 percent of vessel value, up from about 0.4 percent, according to Marsh McLennan data cited by beinsure.com.
For a vessel valued at $100 million, the per-voyage premium rose from approximately $400,000 to approximately $1 million.
Freight rates tell a parallel story.
The spot rate for a Very Large Crude Carrier on the Gulf-to-China route stood at approximately $1.2 million per day in early October, against roughly $80,000 per day a year earlier, according to LSEG data reported by bdnews24 (2026-10-05).
Brent crude settled at $102.94 on 9 October (CNBC, 2026-10-09).
Saudi Arabia’s crude shipments fell to 6 million barrels per day in August, according to the IEA (Trend, 2026-09-14).
Rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope adds weeks to a round trip between the Gulf and northern Europe, and the cost compounds at both ends: higher fuel consumption, elevated insurance for those who still attempt the strait, and reduced effective tanker capacity as ships spend more time at sea.
Capacity removed from the market by longer sailing times is part of what drives the freight rate surge.
The two straits are compounding each other’s costs.

TEHRAN — Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps declared the Strait of Hormuz “closed” on October 26, warning that vessels violating its transit regulations “risk being engulfed in flames,” according to a statement carried by Tasnim News Agency.
The declaration follows IRGC strikes on four tankers accused of conducting unauthorized ship-to-ship oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf on October 22–23, and comes as daily transits through the waterway have fallen from a pre-war baseline of 85 to four, according to IMF PortWatch data published on straits.live.
The announcement turns on a compliance framework Iran has built around its Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a body the United States sanctioned in May 2026 and described as an extortion scheme.
The PGSA requires vessels to register, obtain transit clearance, and use an IRGC-approved corridor near Iran’s coast; ships using the US-promoted southern lane are designated non-compliant.
The authority’s blacklist has grown from 46 named vessels on August 24 to 124 by October 22, according to Lloyd’s List Intelligence.
For vessel operators, the framework creates an impossible bind: registering with the PGSA risks US secondary sanctions under the Office of Foreign Assets Control, while ignoring it risks IRGC attack.
What Changed Between Restriction and Declared Closure
Iran’s enforcement of the strait has escalated through three steps since August.
The PGSA published its first non-compliant vessel list on August 24, naming 46 ships barred from transiting without clearance.
On October 22–23, the IRGC Navy struck four tankers it said were conducting ship-to-ship oil transfers without PGSA authorization — four caught fire, PressTV reported.
Three additional vessels struck mines on the same unauthorized southern route during the same period, PressTV reported.

Free.
See today's issue
On October 23, the IRGC Navy announced that “all movement of non-compliant vessels through the Strait of Hormuz has been completely halted,” CBS News and PressTV reported.
The October 26 statement went further.
“The Strait of Hormuz is closed,” the IRGC stated, per Tasnim News Agency, adding that vessels violating its regulations would be “engulfed in flames.” The identities, flag states, and operators of the four struck vessels have not been publicly confirmed.
IRGC Spokesperson Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi posted on X a photograph of CENTCOM Commander Brad Cooper’s flight over the strait alongside a burning supertanker, captioned “BRENT CRUDE: $117 A BARREL,” Tasnim reported on October 26.
Cooper had stated on October 17, in a video message during his own flyover of the strait, that “the strait is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran,” according to Al Jazeera.
The PGSA Compliance Framework
The IRGC’s enforcement operates through a compliance apparatus with no close precedent in modern maritime confrontations.
Under PGSA rules, as reported by gCaptain and PressTV, vessels must register with the authority, obtain clearance before each transit, and use an IRGC-approved northern corridor near Iran’s coast.
Ships transiting the southern lane — promoted by the US Navy and Oman as the alternative — are classified as non-compliant and subject to interdiction.
The non-compliant vessel list has expanded from 46 ships on August 24 to 124 by October 22, with 43 added in the most recent update, Lloyd’s List Intelligence reported.
Martin Kelly of EOS Risk Group told gCaptain in August that the list is “weighted toward UAE state-linked, Greek-managed, and Indian-linked tonnage, with gas carriers well represented.” The 2026 enforcement regime differs from the 1980s Tanker War, when Iran and Iraq attacked commercial shipping indiscriminately; the IRGC has constructed a quasi-regulatory apparatus — a published authority, a compliance list, stated rules — that gives its enforcement actions a pseudo-legal character, as Al Jazeera noted in an April 2026 analysis.
The IRGC framed the October 22–23 strikes not as military operations but as enforcement against “oil smuggling.” PressTV reported that the IRGC described the struck vessels as engaged in illegal oil transfer operations rather than innocent transit passage — language designed to sidestep the transit passage protections guaranteed under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.
An IRGC Navy statement carried by PressTV and Fars warned: “If oil smuggling resumes, action against non-compliant vessels and the technical systems supporting them will be taken with much greater force.”
What Happens When PGSA Compliance Triggers US Sanctions?
The PGSA framework places vessel operators in a compliance trap with no clean exit.
The US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned the PGSA and warned that companies cooperating with Iranian transit demands — including sharing vessel data or making payments — could face secondary sanctions, gCaptain reported in August.
The warning applied to the very forms of cooperation the PGSA demands: registration, data submission, and payment of transit fees.
For a tanker operator, the options are irreconcilable.
Registering with the PGSA and using the IRGC-approved northern corridor avoids Iranian attack but risks OFAC enforcement.
Ignoring the PGSA and transiting the US-promoted southern lane satisfies US sanctions compliance but invites IRGC interdiction — the four vessels struck on October 22–23 had used the unauthorized route, according to PressTV.
No third option exists for a loaded tanker that needs to exit the Persian Gulf.
The bind extends to the insurance and charter markets.
BIMCO’s CONWARTIME clause, which allows vessel owners to refuse passage through war-risk zones, has been cited in charter agreements for the region.
Lloyd’s List Intelligence reported that 45 former shadow-fleet tankers — vessels that once carried sanctioned Iranian or Russian crude — have moved into mainstream commercial trades, replacing tonnage that can no longer transit the strait.
How Are Shipping and Oil Markets Responding?
The transit data describe a strait that was already functionally closed to most commercial traffic before the IRGC’s formal declaration.
IMF PortWatch recorded four transits on October 18, against a pre-war baseline of 85 per day, according to straits.live.
Oil flows through Hormuz fell to 11.6 million barrels per day in the seven days to October 13 — approximately 68 percent of the pre-war 17.1 million bpd baseline — Kpler data cited by Al Jazeera on October 17 showed.
Non-Iranian-linked vessel transits fell to 81 in the week of October 5–11, down from 105 the previous week, with departures dropping more sharply than arrivals, Lloyd’s List Intelligence reported on October 22.
As of October 26, 92 vessels were holding offshore, according to AIS data on straits.live.
October recorded at least 28 attacks or security incidents in and around the strait — more than double the monthly average since the war began on February 28 — with attacks spreading beyond tankers to containerships, bulk carriers, and gas carriers, Lloyd’s List Intelligence reported.
Brent crude stood at approximately $117 a barrel on October 26, according to the figure cited in Mohebbi’s post as reported by Tasnim — up from approximately $114 earlier in the week.
The market was absorbing simultaneous pressure on both of Saudi Arabia’s export routes: Aramco had told European customers there would be no October oil deliveries, and Saudi Arabia’s overland alternative, the East-West Pipeline, came under Houthi drone attack on the same day the IRGC declared the strait closed.
A CENTCOM spokesperson told Al Jazeera on October 22 that US forces had cleared shipping lanes of mines, that Iran’s mine claims were incorrect, and that 95 percent of vessels were “getting through.” The spokesperson described the IRGC attacks as a sign of Tehran’s “desperation.”
