polymarket-629691.text:
Texas Governor Greg Abbott has moved narrowly ahead of Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa in a new poll, reversing last month’s result as the race enters its final weeks.
The ReconMR survey found that 48 percent of likely Texas voters would support Abbott, a Republican, while 47 percent would back Hinojosa, a state representative.
Some 2 percent selected someone else or said they would not vote, while 3 percent were undecided or declined to answer.
The one-point difference is within the poll’s margin of error, meaning the survey does not establish a clear leader.
Still, it marks a five-point shift from September, when Hinojosa led Abbott by four points, 49 percent to 45 percent.
In an email to Newsweek, Lindsey Hendren, a senior research analyst at ReconMR, cautioned against assuming that the movement represented a decisive change in the race because both surveys remain subject to sampling error.
She said the clearest shift was among independent voters.
Hinojosa led that group by 65 percent to 27 percent in September, a 38-point advantage.
Her lead narrowed to 57 percent to 34 percent in October, cutting the margin to 23 points.
“I think that’s to be debated,” Hendren said when asked whether the statewide movement was meaningful.
She said Abbott’s spending advantage and polling that previously showed him behind may have helped mobilize Republican voters, while emphasizing that “all polls are subject to a margin of sampling error.”
The finding adds to evidence of an unusually competitive contest in a state where Abbott has won three gubernatorial elections.
"The race remains much more competitive than many anticipated earlier this year, or even just a few months ago," Hendren added in a press release on the new poll.
A separate YouGov poll, conducted from September 28 to October 5 among 3,625 likely Texas voters, put Hinojosa one point ahead, 48 percent to 47 percent.
Its margin of error was plus or minus 3 percentage points.
Together, the surveys show the candidates effectively tied rather than demonstrating that either has opened a statistically significant lead.
Newsweek emailed the Abbott and Hinojosa campaigns for comment on Tuesday morning and is awaiting responses.
How Abbott and Hinojosa’s Support Breaks Down
Abbott retains overwhelming support among Republican voters, leading Hinojosa by 92 percent to 5 percent.
Hinojosa leads among Democrats by 94 percent to 2 percent.
Regional figures show Abbott ahead by 25 points in rural Texas.
Hinojosa leads 75 percent to 22 percent in Austin, 52 percent to 44 percent in Houston and 53 percent to 42 percent in San Antonio and South Texas.
The candidates are tied at 48 percent in Dallas-Fort Worth.
Abbott’s job approval rating remains negative, with 48 percent approving and 51 percent disapproving, ReconMR reported.
His favorability rating stands at 46 percent favorable and 50 percent unfavorable.
Hinojosa is viewed favorably by 44 percent and unfavorably by 37 percent, while 20 percent do not know enough about her to offer an opinion.
That represented a marked change from September, when Hinojosa’s rating was 48 percent favorable and 27 percent unfavorable, with 25 percent declining to express an opinion.
Hendren said the closing challenge for Hinojosa was to preserve her advantage among independents while building favorable name recognition.
Abbott, she said, needed to win over more independent voters and improve perceptions of his performance as governor.
Despite the close voting intention numbers, 62 percent of respondents said they expected Abbott to win, compared with 29 percent who predicted a Hinojosa victory.
The Democratic challenger continued campaigning in South Texas during the final stretch, appearing at an October 11 rally in Eagle Pass with Democratic officeholders and candidates.
Her campaign has focused on costs, public education and data-center development, according to a local report on the event in the Eagle Pass Business Journal.
Abbott, meanwhile, campaigned in College Station on October 7 and appeared with law enforcement officials in Arlington the following day, emphasizing Republican turnout and his public-safety platform, according to campaign press releases.
James Talarico Retains Lead Over Ken Paxton
The same ReconMR poll placed Democrat James Talarico four points ahead of Republican Ken Paxton in the U.S.
Senate race, 48 percent to 44 percent.
That represented a slight narrowing from September, when Talarico led 49 percent to 43 percent.
The difference is also within the survey’s margin of error.
Talarico led among Democrats by 92 percent to 2 percent, while Paxton held an 87 percent to 7 percent advantage among Republicans.
Likely independent voters favored Talarico by 60 percent to 30 percent.
Regionally, Talarico led by 74 percent to 21 percent in Austin and by 56 percent to 38 percent in San Antonio and South Texas.
His advantage in the latter region had narrowed from 33 points in September to 18 points in October.
Paxton led by 18 points in rural Texas, while the candidates were virtually even in Houston and Talarico held a slight Dallas-Fort Worth edge, according to ReconMR.
Talarico’s favorability rating stood at 48 percent favorable and 43 percent unfavorable, down from 50 percent to 39 percent in September.
Paxton was viewed favorably by 40 percent and unfavorably by 55 percent.

Election 2026: Iowa Senate race tightens with less than two weeks to Election Day
Polls show no clear front-runner between Hinson and Turek as spending nears record levels
DES MOINES, Iowa (WOWT) - Iowa’s Senate candidates are making their final pitch to voters with less than two weeks left before Election Day.
A review of the top 12 preferred polls from The New York Times on the race shows no clear-cut leader.
Seven of the 12 polls favor Republican Ashley Hinson, while five favor Democrat Josh Turek.
Candidates campaign across the state
Hinson campaigned in Glenwood on Wednesday with Sen.
Joni Ernst, who is not seeking re-election.
Turek held an event in Council Bluffs on Tuesday.
Both candidates addressed prices, including health care costs.
“There is more to do to lower prices.
I think that there are a lot of Iowans who have been priced out of the American dream,” Hinson said.
“I want to fight for affordable and accessible pharmaceuticals.
I think it’s wrong to live in the richest country on Earth, and people can’t afford to take their medicine,” Turek said.
Analyst points to competitive race
Political analyst Dave Price said the tight race is surprising.
“If you step back and maybe turn back the clock, you would think this is probably not going to be a super competitive race just because of what’s happened in the state over the past decade, where Republican candidates, frankly, have just done so much better,” Price said.
Price said rising costs and the war with Iran are important issues to voters.
“The war with Iran, inflation going up, people keep driving by gas stations and seeing how much more expensive it is.
Their groceries are more expensive.
All of those things, the cost of living, that all really kind of factor into the unpopularity of Donald Trump,” Price said.
Spending expected to break records
Price said spending in the race is on pace to be unprecedented.
“That Senate race, that’s clearly going to be more money than we’ve ever seen spent on a United States Senate race in Iowa history.
There is so much outside money, which just underscores how much each major political party wants to win this seat since it is an open seat,” Price said.
Both campaigns are expected to continue crisscrossing the state through Election Day.
Libertarian Thomas Lane is also on the ballot.

polymarket-630747.text:
Kansas' Senate race is showing signs of becoming more competitive than Republicans might have expected in a state where Democrats haven't won a Senate seat in nearly a century.
A new Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media survey gives Democrat Adam Hamilton a 45 percent to 43 percent lead over Republican Senator Roger Marshall, with libertarian David Graham at 4 percent.
The September 15-16 poll is the first independent survey this cycle to show Hamilton ahead.
Marshall is seeking a second term, while Hamilton, the founder of the country's largest United Methodist Church, is trying to become the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Kansas since 1932.
Vice President JD Vance is scheduled to make a stop in Olathe, Kansas, on Monday to show support for Marshall.
Newsweek reached out to Hamilton and Marshall campaigns for comment Friday.
Marshall remains the favorite, though the latest Emerson College poll suggests the race could be closer than many expect.
“This poll finds Democrats with their best chance to win their first Senate seat in Kansas since 1932, in part driven by Democrat Hamilton’s appeal to independent voters, leading by 15 points,” said Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling.
An earlier co/efficient poll, conducted September 8-10 among 915 likely voters, had Marshall leading Hamilton 49 percent to 44 percent, with 5 percent undecided.
The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.22 percentage points.
Other recent surveys have shown a tighter race.
A Global Strategy Group poll conducted August 12-16 among 800 likely voters found Hamilton narrowly ahead, 44 percent to 43 percent.
The one-point difference was within the poll's margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points.
Another August poll showed Marshall with a narrow lead.
A Public Policy Polling survey conducted August 7-8 had Marshall ahead 46 percent to 45 percent.
The available results do not report a margin of error.
Election forecasters have said the Senate race in Kansas has become more competitive since Hamilton won the Democratic nomination in August, though Marshall is still favored to win.
The Cook Political Report shifted the contest from "solid Republican" to "likely Republican" after Hamilton’s primary win.
Independents and the Issues Behind the Numbers
The Emerson poll points to independents as the reason the race is close.
Hamilton leads that group 42 percent to 27 percent, according to the poll, while independents in the governor's race break for Republican Ty Masterson by two points.
Favorability ratings are close to a wash.
Marshall is underwater, 41 percent favorable to 48 percent unfavorable.
Hamilton's numbers are better on paper, 41 percent favorable to 30 percent unfavorable, though 13 percent still don't know enough about him to have an opinion, a gap that could move either direction before November.
The poll also found President Trump's approval rating in Kansas at 40 percent, with 53 percent disapproving.
Governor Laura Kelly's approval sits at 46 percent.
The economy is the top issue for Kansas voters at 48 percent, well ahead of healthcare, threats to democracy, housing affordability, education and immigration.
Cook Political Report moved the race from Solid Republican to Likely Republican on August 5, shortly after Hamilton won the Democratic primary.
The state has a Cook Partisan Voting Index of R+8.
Fifty Plus One also rates the race Lean Republican, though its forecast gives Marshall a larger edge.
Kansas remains a strongly Republican state.
Trump won the state by 16.1 points in 2024, up from 14.7 points in 2020.
The state's electorate is also heavily white and non-college-educated, groups that have generally leaned Republican in recent elections.
A Red State With a Blue Governor
Kansas has given Republicans a long run of Senate victories, and Marshall has never lost a race by more than single digits.
But the state’s political history is more complicated once voters get beyond the Senate.
Kelly has won two terms, and a 2022 ballot measure that would have removed abortion protections from the state constitution was rejected by 59 percent of voters.
Marshall is leaning into the Republican coalition that has carried the state for decades, focusing on rural voters and warning that a Hamilton victory could help Democrats take control of the Senate.
Hamilton, meanwhile, is presenting himself as a centrist.
He points to his own congregation, which he says is split roughly evenly among Democrats, Republicans and independents, as an example of the voters he hopes to bring into his campaign.
Who Is Adam Hamilton?
Hamilton, a first-time candidate, founded Church of the Resurrection in Leawood, the nation’s largest United Methodist Church.
He built his church from a few members meeting in a funeral home chapel in 1990 into a 25,000-member congregation with nine locations across the Kansas City area.
He has written more than 30 books, mostly on Christian theology.
He won the Democratic nomination in August after campaigning as a faith-based moderate who could compete in conservative Kansas.
He raised $3.6 million during the first two months of his campaign, leading Democrats to argue that the Senate race in Kansas could be more competitive than expected this year.
Marshall has branded Hamilton as "too woke for Kansas."
But Hamilton described himself as a centrist, running partly on "bringing people together." His congregation is nearly evenly split between Democrats, Republicans and independents, he said.
Roger Marshall Sues Patients: What To Know
Marshall sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills ranging from as little as $101 to several thousand dollars over his decades-long medical career, The New York Times reported.
Authorities arrested about 81 patients after they missed court appearances related to those cases.
About half the lawsuits were filed under Marshall's name, and the rest were filed by Heartland Regional OBGYN, the Great Bend medical practice that Marshall solely owned from 1998 to 2012 and then co-owned until 2019.
Most of the patients who were sued lived in Barton County, a rural area where the rates of uninsured people and poverty are above-average, according to the Times.
The patients were reportedly routinely charged an 18 percent annual interest rate on outstanding bills, and some had their bank accounts garnished.
Steven Johnson, an attorney who often represented Marshall in debt cases, told the Times that the warrants and arrests were necessary to ensure debtors attended court dates.
"If defendants were allowed to appear only when they wanted to without any consequences the court would get no business done," he said.
Marshall's campaign defended his record, arguing that he had long treated patients regardless of their ability to pay and that judges, not doctors, issued warrants.
Payton Fuller, a spokeswoman for Marshall's campaign, said the hospital "provided millions in uncompensated care" and "used the exact same billing and outside collection procedures as every other business or hospital in Kansas."

polymarket-630747.text:
Democrats have their eyes on a potential upset in Kansas, where recent polls show the U.S.
Senate race in a dead heat and the Cook Political Report rates the contest Lean Republican with roughly four weeks until Election Day.
The position is held by Republican incumbent Senator Roger Marshall, a doctor, who is battling Democrat Adam Hamilton for the seat that has been held by the GOP since 1919, the longest ever for any party, High Plains Public Radio says.
Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them.
Republicans now hold a narrow majority in both the House and Senate.
President Donald Trump carried Kansas by double digits over then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election, underscoring the state’s Republican tilt.
But Democrats have maintained a foothold in the state, with Laura Kelly in the governor’s mansion even as Republicans hold both U.S.
Senate seats.
Newsweek reached out to both Marshall and Hamilton's campaigns via email on Monday for comment.
What To Know
According to recent polling, Hamilton either leads by a very slim margin or the race is statistically tied.
Cook says Hamilton is running an "increasingly strong race" and has been launching an attack ad against Marshall, an OB-GYN, over billing and collection practices at his office.
Marshall has branded the ad targeting his practice a "lie." The forecaster also highlights that agriculture—and economic concerns impacting fertilizer and gas—are major factors in the Sunflower State and the rising prices make the race more competitive.
Meanwhile, Marshall has branded Hamilton as a "radical Democrat," adding that "his sermons are identical to the Democratic Party platform."
Democrats are hoping to capitalize on Trump's dropping approval ratings in state and national polls as the midterm elections loom.
The president's overall approval and ranking on key policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have slipped as households across America are flagging affordability concerns.
Robert Y.
Shapiro, professor of political science at the School of International and Public Affairs at Columbia, told Newsweek on Monday when asked if Democrats realistically could flip the seat: "If this is a 'Wave' election it can flip.
Or even otherwise since Hamilton is a very good moderate Democrat running against a very vulnerable opponent.
This would be then a one off election unless this establishes a viable precedent for future Democratic candidates in Kansas.
And possibly for Democrats elsewhere."
What the Polls Show
In a poll by The New York Times and Siena University last month, Marshall had 47 percent of the potential vote compared to 46 percent for Hamilton, and 7 percent of respondents said they did not know.
The poll surveyed 605 likely voters from September 22 to September 30 and had a margin of error of 4.6 points.
A Trafalgar Group poll shows Hamilton has 44.4 percent of the potential vote compared to 43.5 percent for Marshall, 2 percent for Libertarian Party candidate David C Graham and 10.1 percent are undecided.
The poll surveyed 1,095 likely voters across the state from September 29 to October 1 and has a margin of error of 2.9 percent.
Breakdown of Hamilton vs.
Marshall
Hamilton is pastor of the largest United Methodist Church in the country, the Church of the Resurrection.
He founded the Kansas City-area church in 1990 at age 25, according to his campaign website.
He won the Democratic Senate primary in August and is running on affordability; a theme Democrats across the country are emphasizing.
His campaign is focused on bringing down energy, housing and healthcare costs as well as protecting Social Security, agriculture and ending “chaos and corruption” in Washington, D.C., his website says.
Meanwhile, Marshall has been in the U.S.
Senate since winning his 2020 election.
He has been an OB-GYN in the state for 25 years, his campaign website highlights, and calls himself a fifth-generation "farm kid."
Trump endorsed Marshall, labeling him a "strong advocate" for the people of Kansas.
His campaign website touts bills from agriculture, border security and rural healthcare as a guide for voters to see what policies are important to the Republican.

polymarket-630924.text:
The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, announced three Senate rating changes on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, two weeks before Election Day.
It moved Minnesota’s open-seat race from “Likely Democrat” to “Lean Democrat,” a shift toward Republican nominee Michele Tafoya.
It also moved South Carolina from “Likely Republican” to “Lean Republican” and Mississippi from “Solid Republican” to “Likely Republican,” both toward Democrats.
◉ Key Facts
- ►Minnesota: Likely Democrat to Lean Democrat (toward Republicans), in the race between Democratic Lt.
Gov.
Peggy Flanagan and Republican Michele Tafoya.
- ►South Carolina: Likely Republican to Lean Republican (toward Democrats), with Democrat Annie Andrews facing Sen.
Darline Graham.
- ►Mississippi: Solid Republican to Likely Republican (toward Democrats), with Sen.
Cindy Hyde-Smith facing Democrat Scott Colom and independent Ty Pinkins.
- ►Cook’s Senate and Governors Editor Jessica Taylor attributed the moves to candidate quality, which she said can be magnified in ways that defy national trends.
- ►The midterm elections are on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, 14 days after the announcement.
The announcement is a rare two-directional adjustment in the closing stretch of the campaign.
The moves give each party something to be hopeful about in the homestretch, with Republicans hoping to flip the open Minnesota seat being vacated by retiring Sen.
Tina Smith (D), and Democrats suddenly seeing a new opportunity in South Carolina.
Taylor wrote that in Senate races, the quality of individual candidates can be magnified in ways that defy national trends, especially in midterm years.
The forecaster said the shifts do not change our overall outlook for the Senate.
In Minnesota, Cook’s analysis pointed to the state’s welfare fraud scandal as a driver of Republican optimism.
Republicans have been bullish on Minnesota for months and hope voters’ concerns about corruption will stick to Flanagan; Cook said recent polling has shown her slightly underperforming given the national environment.
The rating change is notable because it has been one of the only Senate shifts in favor of Republicans from major election forecasters so far this cycle.
Tafoya is a longtime television sports reporter making her first run for public office; recent polls have shown the contest tightening, with some putting the candidates within the margin of error.
The two met Friday for their only scheduled debate, in which Tafoya sought to hold Flanagan responsible for fraud scandals plaguing Minnesota state programs, while Flanagan challenged Tafoya over her ties to President Donald Trump.
| State | Previous Rating | New Rating | Direction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Minnesota | Likely Democrat | Lean Democrat | Toward GOP |
| South Carolina | Likely Republican | Lean Republican | Toward Democrats |
| Mississippi | Solid Republican | Likely Republican | Toward Democrats |
South Carolina’s shift follows an unusual sequence of events: the late Sen.
Lindsey Graham died on July 11, 2026, and his sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to the seat on July 13, 2026; she is the Republican nominee in November.
Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, is running against Graham and, per the report, has been campaigning for the seat and raising her profile since May of last year.
Cook’s analysis said both the South Carolina and Mississippi races feature unique factors that are making each more competitive than it should be.
Cook described the two moves as further evidence that Democrats have expanded the map into red territory even in the Deep South.
In Mississippi, incumbent Sen.
Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican from Brookhaven, faces Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee and a district attorney from Columbus, and Ty Pinkins, an independent and Army veteran.
The race has attracted millions in spending from political action committees and outside groups.
Separately, Senate Majority PAC announced a $1.2 million ad campaign in the state through Election Day.
Some observers have noted that Pinkins’s presence on the ballot could draw votes away from the Democratic nominee.
📚 Background & Context
Minnesota has not elected a Republican to the Senate since Norm Coleman in 2002, and Kamala Harris carried the state by more than four points in 2024.
In Mississippi, the state hasn’t sent a Democrat to the U.S.
Senate since John Stennis in 1982, and Trump won it by nearly 23 points in 2024.
No U.S.
senator from Mississippi has been unseated since 1942.
When Cook moves a race so that it is leaning in one party’s direction, it is just one lane away from being a toss-up.
Thirty-five Senate seats are on the November 3, 2026 ballot.
Ratings from forecasters are analytical judgments, not predictions of certain outcomes, and they can diverge across organizations.
Ratings can shift quickly in the final weeks.
Observers will be watching further polling, candidate spending, and any additional rating changes before voters go to the polls on November 3, 2026.
💬 What People Are Saying
Based on public reaction across social media and news platforms, here is the general consensus on this story:
- 🔴Conservative voices emphasized the Minnesota shift as validation of concerns about the state’s fraud scandals and Tafoya’s outsider profile, while downplaying the South Carolina and Mississippi moves as candidate-specific and unlikely to flip deep-red seats.
- 🔵Liberal voices highlighted the South Carolina and Mississippi moves as evidence of an expanding Democratic map amid frustration over prices and the Iran war, while noting Minnesota remains rated as leaning Democratic.
- 🟠Many observers saw the changes as a reminder that ratings are snapshots, that all three seats remain favored for the incumbent party, and that turnout over the final two weeks will decide the outcomes.
Note: Social reactions represent general public sentiment and do not reflect Political.org’s editorial position.

(AP) — Dr.
Annie Andrews, the South Carolina Democrat who unsuccessfully challenged U.S.
Rep.
Nancy Mace in 2022, says she's running against Republican U.S.
Sen.
Lindsey Graham in 2026, challenging the four-term incumbent in part due to what she characterized as his waffling positions over the course of his political career.
“He’s changed his position on nearly every issue over that time and that’s because, in my view, he doesn’t stand for anything or believe in anything other than what it takes to get reelected,” Andrews, a pediatrician in Charleston, told The Associated Press before a campaign rollout Thursday.
Andrews joins at least one other Democrat in a primary field.
In her launch video, Andrews says it’s “embarrassing” to see how politicians like Graham — at the moment one of President Donald Trump’s top Senate allies — have swung from criticizing Trump to working to gain his favor.
The video features archival video of Graham bemoaning critics who called Trump a “kook” and then, a year earlier, using the same term to describe his former GOP primary foe in the 2016 presidential contest.
MORE | "Dr.
Annie Andrews announces South Carolina senate bid, set to challenge Lindsey Graham."
Andrews also levies criticism at Graham for voting to confirm Trump’s Cabinet picks and for his relationship with Elon Musk, describing “an unelected billionaire ...
taking a chainsaw to Social Security, Medicare and veterans’ healthcare.” She calls Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth “a guy who can’t even organize a text thread,” a reference to the recent Signal chat scandal in which war plans were discussed.
No Democrat has won a U.S.
Senate seat in South Carolina in decades, and Republicans in recent history typically take statewide seats by double-digit margins.
When he last ran in 2020, Graham defeated his Democratic opponent, Jaime Harrison, by a 10 percentage point margin.
That contest turned into South Carolina’s most expensive ever, with both candidates posting record fundraising that surpassed $200 million total and continued to grow in the race’s closing days.
Harrison, who went on to chair the Democratic National Committee, became the first U.S.
Senate candidate to amass a war chest of more than $100 million over the course of the race.
Andrews was the Democratic nominee who unsuccessfully sought to unseat Mace in 2022, losing to the Republican by 14 percentage points.
South Carolina's 1st District, which spans the state's southern coast, is the only one to have flipped from red to blue in decades, when Joe Cunningham won it for Democrats for a single term in the 2018 election.
Mace won it in 2020 and has been reelected twice, although in 2026 she is eyeing a race for governor.
In the years since her House run, Andrews stepped away from her practice at the Medical University of South Carolina and founded a political organization focused on issues related to children, including climate change, gun violence and childhood poverty.
According to federal filings, an affiliated political action committee, Their Future PAC, gave $7,000 to a handful of candidates in the 2024 cycle and had about $5,000 on hand at the end of 2024.
Asked about Democrats' lackluster statewide record in the state, Andrews said she felt Harrison's effort was “hamstrung” by necessary precautions in place during the pandemic.
Now, she said, voters feel strained under the effects of the Trump administration's “chaotic” policies.
"Lindsey Graham has had 22 years to make things better for folks here in South Carolina, and I think you'd be hard-pressed to find many voters who could articulate in what way Lindsey has made their life better," Andrews said.
Graham, seeking his fifth Senate term, kicked off his reelection campaign in February, announcing that Gov.
Henry McMaster and Sen.
Tim Scott would chair his effort.
Scott, the state’s junior senator, is serving as chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the chamber’s campaign arm.
At least one Republican has announced a primary challenge to Graham.

4 candidates set for South Carolina’s US Senate race in November
COLUMBIA, S.C.
(WRDW/WAGT) - Four candidates will appear on the U.S.
Senate general election ballot in South Carolina this November: incumbent Darline Graham, Annie Andrews, Kasie Whitener and Mark Hackett.
None of the four candidates has ever won statewide office or a seat in the state House, the traditional launch pad to Washington, making this race look different from past Senate contests.
Graham won the Republican nomination by 5 points Tuesday night, setting the November ballot.
She has pledged loyalty to President Donald Trump and says she’ll focus on affordability and issues in South Carolina if elected.
“Liberals believe if they can defeat conservatives in South Carolina then they can defeat us anywhere.
Once again, they’re coming for us and the South Carolina values we hold dear,” Graham said.
Democrat Annie Andrews, a Lowcountry pediatrician, hopes to become the first Democrat South Carolina sends to the U.S.
Senate since Fritz Hollings, who retired in the early 2000s.
Andrews repeatedly criticized Graham in an interview, saying Graham isn’t ready for the job.
She calls herself a voice in the middle as both parties drift farther left and right.
“One of the lessons I’ve learned is the far left can keep talking to each other, the far right can keep talking to each other, but we’re never going to get anything done unless we start talking to each other in the center, and that’s what I intend to do,” Andrews said.
Libertarian Kasie Whitener says the two-party system is broken, arguing candidates care more about pleasing their party than serving constituents.
“That’s what we’re trying to offer is a vision of opportunity leadership, focus on entrepreneurship and reform at that high federal level,” Whitener said.
News 12 reached out to Mark Hackett, running under the Constitution Party.
He did not respond.

Darline Graham Tied in Senate Race, Opponent’s Shock Internal Poll Claims
Dr.
Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee for South Carolina’s U.S.
Senate seat, released an internal poll Tuesday her pollster says shows she “has a chance to pull off a major upset” against Sen.
Darline Graham (R-SC), who was appointed to finish her late brother Sen.
Lindsey Graham’s (R-SC) term.
The polling memo from Impact Research is clearly targeted at a national audience, hoping to encourage Democratic donors to throw some financial support behind Andrews’ bid to win a state that voted for President Donald Trump by an 18-point margin.
The poll was conducted from Aug.
18 to Aug.
24 among 700 likely voters with a margin of error of +/- 3.7%.
When asked who they planned to vote for, the Democrat and Republican were tied, with 41% each, Libertarian candidate Kasie Whitener pulling 5%, and 13% undecided.
The pollster then read a “positive bio” for both Andrews and Graham and asked respondents again who they would vote for senator.
The bios were as follows:
Dr.
Annie Andrews, a Democrat, is a mom and pediatrician.
After nearly fifteen years caring for sick kids at the Children’s Hospital in Charleston, she saw how Washington’s corruption hurt kids and families while special interests and career politicians benefit.
Andrews is running for Senate to fight for affordable healthcare, lower grocery and prescription drug prices, and take on Washington by passing term limits on all politicians, banning insider stock trading by members of Congress, and she’ll refuse corporate PAC money.
Darline Graham, a Republican, is South Carolina’s first female Senator and Lindsey Graham’s sister, appointed to carry on her brother’s legacy in the seat he held for over two decades.
She’s been endorsed by President Trump and Senator Tim Scott for her strong conservative values and commitment to South Carolina.
In the Senate, she’ll cut out-of-control spending, lower taxes, and secure the border to keep our streets safe.
After hearing that information, the choices shifted in Andrews’ favor, with 44% picking her, 39% Graham, 4% Whitener, and 13% undecided.
With Independent voters, Andrews led by 33 points in the original question and by 39 points after hearing the two bios.
The pollster characterized this as Andrews “solidifying her Democratic base and winning over voters in the middle by large margins.”
The poll highlighted Andrews’ stronger favorability ratings as well, with 36% favorable and 21% unfavorable image; among Independents, Andrews was even stronger, with a +24 favorability.
Graham was the opposite and “saddled with negative baggage,” the pollster wrote, with 36% favorable and 49% unfavorable, and far underwater with Independents at -47 favorability.
Graham may have won the primary, but is struggling to win over the GOP base, the pollster added, at 53% favorable and 32% unfavorable among Republicans.
The pollster — which, again, was hired by the Andrews campaign, and is not neutral — argued that this was “not a conventional red-state long shot” and the “seat is very much in play.” Impact Research’s reasoning was that Andrews was more “appealing to voters” and Graham was a “weak incumbent” who is “deeply unpopular” and has “an overwhelming amount of baggage.”
If Andrews is able to garner the ” proper resources to both defend her values and highlight Graham’s weaknesses,” meaning campaign donations, she “has a chance to pull off a major upset,” the pollster wrote, describing this race as an “opportunity” that was “worth national investment.”
Darline Graham became a senator after her older brother, the incumbent, died unexpectedly at the age of 71 on July 11, shortly after winning his primary.
She was appointed by South Carolina Gov.
Henry McMaster(R) — at Trump’s enthusiastic urging — to finish her brother’s term and sworn into office on July 14.
Trump soon declared he was encouraging Graham to run for the seat and posted a “Complete and Total Endorsement” for her on his Truth Social account, but that was not sufficient to clear the field for her.
Eleven other Republicans filed to run for the Aug.
11 special primary election, including Rep.
Ralph Norman (R-SC), Rep.
Russell Fry (R-SC), and former South Carolina congressman and governor Mark Sanford.
Graham and Norman advanced to a runoff, and despite a disastrous debate performance by Graham, she scored the win and advanced to face Andrews in the general.
Norman expressed bitterness after the defeat, calling Trump’s decision to endorse in the primary “shocking” and even suggesting that Republicans should vote for him as a write-in on the general election ballot.
He later walked that back and said he would support Graham in November, but his critiques of Graham reflect those voiced by other South Carolina Republicans.
